Grignard reaction. A fundamental organometallic chemical reaction in which alkyl, allyl, vinyl, or aryl-magnesium halides—known as Grignard reagents—react as nucleophiles with carbon electrophiles, most commonly carbonyl compounds. This reaction is one of the most powerful methods for creating carbon-carbon bonds, converting aldehydes and ketones into secondary and tertiary alcohols, respectively. Victor Grignard discovered this reaction and was awarded the 1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work. It is characterized by a polar covalent carbon-magnesium bond that reverses the typical electrophilic nature of carbon. Because Grignard reagents are highly basic and nucleophilic, the reaction must be performed under strictly anhydrous conditions in ether solvents to prevent immediate protonation and decomposition.

Grignard reagents are synthesized by reacting an organic halide, such as bromobenzene or iodomethane, with magnesium metal in an anhydrous ether solvent, typically diethyl ether or tetrahydrofuran. This involves the insertion of magnesium into the carbon-halogen bond, reversing the carbon's polarization—a process called umpolung—to make it highly nucleophilic and basic. The reagents require strictly anhydrous conditions because they react violently with proton donors, including water, alcohols, and carboxylic acids, to form simple alkanes and magnesium salts. In solution, the organomagnesium halide exhibits the Schlenk equilibrium, a complex coordination dynamic where the organomagnesium halide exists in equilibrium with dialkylmagnesium and magnesium halide species.

Grignard reagents react with formaldehyde to yield primary alcohols after acid workup, extending the carbon chain by one carbon atom. They react with other aldehydes to synthesize secondary alcohols and with ketones to yield tertiary alcohols. When reacting with esters or acid chlorides in a two-equivalent addition, the nucleophile attacks twice to produce a tertiary alcohol with two identical groups. The reagents also react with carbon dioxide—often dry ice—to produce carboxylic acids after acidic workup, a carboxylation process that adds a carboxyl group to the chain. They react with epoxides by attacking the less substituted carbon, opening the ring to yield a primary alcohol extended by two carbons.

The Grignard reaction exemplifies the concept of umpolung, changing an electrophilic carbon in an alkyl halide to a nucleophilic one. Grignard reagents are prepared directly from organic halides, and the primary product of their additions to carbonyl compounds is an alcohol. The key transition-group metal involved is magnesium, which inserts into the carbon-halogen bond to form the organometallic reagent.
